chapters.title: Cold Open
chapters.text:
Throw a tennis ball at a brick wall, and you already know how the story ends. It bounces back, every single time.

In the subatomic world, though, those rules break. An electron or a radioactive particle can act like a wave and slip straight through a solid energy barrier it has no business crossing — a phenomenon called quantum tunneling.

For decades, physicists assumed that trick belonged exclusively to single atoms and invisible particles. Then, the twenty twenty-five Nobel Prize in Physics honored an experiment that shattered that boundary.

Using a superconducting electrical circuit on a chip big enough to hold in the palm of your hand, three physicists watched an entire circuit sitting calmly at zero voltage suddenly tunnel straight through a barrier and snap into a voltage state — behaving, all at once, like a single giant atom.

chapters.title: Billions Moving as One
chapters.text:
Wait — why can't a tennis ball tunnel through a wall in the first place?

Because a tennis ball isn't one quantum object. It is trillions of trillions of atoms all vibrating, colliding, and jiggling out of sync. Even if one atom tries to act like a wave, its neighbors instantly scramble it.

To see quantum behavior at human scale, you somehow need billions of particles to stop acting like a chaotic crowd and start moving like a single synchronized dancer.

That is what happens inside a superconductor. Cool a metal like niobium close to absolute zero, and electrons stop bouncing off the crystal lattice. Instead, they bind together into Cooper pairs. And here is the magic: unlike ordinary electrons that refuse to share the same state, billions of Cooper pairs drop into the exact same quantum wave, marching in total lockstep across the whole chip.

Now, back in nineteen sixty-two, Brian Josephson already proved that individual Cooper pairs can tunnel across a razor-thin insulating gap between two superconductors. That was microscopic tunneling — one pair at a time.

In nineteen eighty, theorist Anthony Leggett asked something far bolder: could the entire electrical state of the whole circuit — billions of pairs locked together as one single variable — tunnel straight through a barrier all at once?

chapters.title: The Tilted Washboard
chapters.text:
To test Leggett's challenge, you need a way to trap that collective wave and watch it escape.

The centerpiece is a Josephson junction: two superconducting metal strips crossing over an insulating oxide sheet only a few atoms thick, forming a tiny square about a tenth the width of a human hair.

Inside that junction, the billions of synchronized Cooper pairs share one single electrical property — the phase difference across the gap. And here is the clearest way to picture how that phase behaves: imagine a marble sitting inside a bumpy washboard of hills and valleys.

When no current flows, the washboard lies flat, and the marble sits peacefully at the bottom of a valley.

Now slowly dial up a steady electric current through the circuit. As the current climbs — up toward just under ten microamps — the entire washboard tilts. Look closely at what happens to the valley: the hill in front of the marble gets shorter and thinner, but it is still a real barrier.

As long as the marble stays trapped inside that pocket, the phase cannot move, and the voltage across the chip stays strictly zero. Current glides right through with zero voltage drop.

But the exact microsecond that marble escapes its pocket, it starts tumbling rapidly down the tilted hills — and suddenly, a sharp measurable voltage snaps onto the wires.

chapters.title: The Saboteur in the Wires
chapters.text:
Sounds clean on paper — so why didn't anyone prove it immediately?

Actually, in nineteen eighty-one, researchers at IBM saw tantalizing hints that a junction kept switching even at ultra-low temperatures. But skeptics had a brutal objection.

Your chip might be sitting near absolute zero, yet metal wires still have to run down from your room-temperature laboratory to measure it. Every warm wire radiates invisible room-temperature microwaves. Those stray ripples can race straight down the cable and violently kick the marble right over the top of the hill — perfectly mimicking quantum tunneling when nothing quantum happened at all.

In nineteen eighty-four at UC Berkeley, professor John Clarke, postdoc Michel Devoret, and PhD student John Martinis decided to eliminate every possible excuse.

First, they built an ingenious shield right into the cold wiring: tiny tubes packed solid with microscopic insulated copper powder. Smooth direct current glided right through, while stray high-frequency microwaves smashed into millions of conductive copper grains and died out completely.

Second, before cooling into the quantum zone, they measured every single electrical property of their junction right inside the warm classical regime. That left zero adjustable fudge factors. Once the chip got cold, quantum theory made one rigid, unchangeable prediction — either nature hit the bullseye, or it didn't.

chapters.title: Tunneling Through the Hill
chapters.text:
Then they fired up the dilution refrigerator and watched the marble escape, thousands of times in a row.

When the chip was relatively warm — around a hundred millikelvin — heat energy rattled the marble until it hopped over the top of the hill. Cool the fridge down, and the thermal rattle shrinks, so escapes get dramatically rarer.

On a chart of the circuit's effective escape temperature against the fridge's actual temperature, the data marched cleanly down a straight diagonal line. Until thirty millikelvin.

Right there, the curve broke away and went completely flat. Even as they chilled the refrigerator all the way down to nineteen millikelvin — more than a hundred times colder than deep space — the circuit kept escaping as if stuck at thirty-seven millikelvin, landing squarely on the zero-parameter quantum tunneling prediction.

Still, a great experimentalist never stops there. What if the thermometer was lying, or stray noise was still heating the chip to thirty-seven millikelvin?

In nineteen eighty-five, the Berkeley team pulled off a checkmate control test. They turned on a gentle magnetic field across the chip. That magnetic field lowered the junction's critical current, pushing the predicted quantum crossover below nineteen millikelvin.

Instantly, the flat plateau vanished — and the escape rate dropped straight back down to nineteen millikelvin, matching the thermometer. There was no hidden noise floor. The entire macroscopic circuit was genuinely tunneling straight through the barrier.

chapters.title: The First Artificial Atom
chapters.text:
Yet Clarke, Devoret, and Martinis went one giant step further. If billions of Cooper pairs trapped in that valley truly behave as one quantum particle, tunneling isn't the only signature you should see.

Inside an atom, an electron cannot hold just any arbitrary amount of energy — it can only occupy discrete, quantized rungs on an energy ladder.

So in a companion nineteen eighty-five experiment, the Berkeley team aimed gentle microwaves — at two gigahertz — directly at the trapped circuit.

If the circuit were classical, it would absorb energy smoothly across a broad smudge. Instead, as they slowly swept the bias current, the tunnel escape rate stayed quiet… and then erupted in three razor-sharp resonant peaks.

One peak where a microwave photon kicked the circuit from the ground state up to rung one. A second peak from rung one to rung two. And a third from rung two to rung three.

Because higher rungs sit closer to the top of the hill where the barrier is drastically thinner, every jump made the circuit tunnel out dramatically faster — letting the team actually see each discrete quantum level.

A centimeter-sized electrical circuit, etched onto silicon by human hands, was absorbing light in discrete quantum packets just like a single hydrogen atom. Humanity had built its first macroscopic artificial atom.

If watching a hand-sized chip act like a single giant atom just blew your mind, take a second to hit that like button — because hidden inside those three peaks is the exact reason modern quantum computers exist at all.

chapters.title: Why Uneven Rungs Built Qubits
chapters.text:
Look back closely at those three peaks from nineteen eighty-five, because hidden inside them is the exact reason modern superconducting quantum computers exist at all.

Suppose you tried to build a quantum bit out of an ordinary superconducting coil and capacitor — a classic linear circuit. Even if you cooled it near absolute zero, its energy valley is a perfectly symmetric bowl, which means every single rung on its ladder is spaced by the exact same energy gap.

Try sending a microwave pulse to flip your bit cleanly from zero to one, and that exact same pulse will immediately kick it from one to two, and two to three. You can never isolate a clean two-level qubit.

A Josephson junction breaks that symmetry. Because its energy valley curves unevenly, the spacing between rungs shrinks as you climb. The jump from zero to one takes a slightly different microwave frequency than the jump from one to two.

That tiny mismatch is pure gold: it lets engineers tune a microwave pulse that talks exclusively to zero and one while ignoring every higher state completely.

Over the next decades, physicists turned that Berkeley artificial atom into full quantum bits — from early Cooper-pair boxes in nineteen ninety-nine, to John Martinis's phase qubits, to the transmon architecture Michel Devoret helped pioneer at Yale in two thousand seven, which powers today's leading superconducting quantum processors.

chapters.title: The Fragile Edge of Reality
chapters.text:
There is one last crucial twist that keeps this physics grounded in reality.

In their follow-up tests, Clarke, Devoret, and Martinis also verified a haunting prediction by Amir Caldeira and Anthony Leggett: connect even a tiny trace of electrical friction — ordinary resistance — to the junction, and the environment continuously eavesdrops on the phase state.

Like dragging that marble through thick honey, dissipation chokes off macroscopic tunneling exponentially. That is why the quantum world feels invisible in everyday life, and why modern quantum computers still hang inside massive golden dilution refrigerators cooled below fifteen millikelvin, fighting every stray photon, magnetic ripple, and microscopic chip defect.

The nineteen eighty-five Berkeley experiment didn't magically put a baseball in two places at once — later experiments in two thousand pushed even further into macroscopic superpositions of opposing currents.

What Clarke, Devoret, and Martinis proved — and what earned the twenty twenty-five Nobel Prize in Physics — is something deeper. Quantum mechanics does not expire at the edge of an atom. The wall separating the quantum world from objects you can hold in your hand was never a law of nature. It was just noise.
